fixes.find: my helmet knocks against the props, tok, tok, like a stick along a fence.
fixes.replace: my helmet knocks against the props, knock, knock, like a stick dragged along a fence.
fixes.why: English onomatopoeia and the simile need a verb; the original wording reads transliterated.

fixes.find: I stood that minute out next to Mikhalych, listening.
fixes.replace: I spent that minute standing next to Mikhalych, listening.
fixes.why: Literal Russian word order/verb choice; this is the idiomatic English phrasing.

fixes.find: Seryoga by the drive, by the way, they dug out alive; I remember that too, from somewhere.
fixes.replace: By the way, they dug Seryoga out alive by the drive; I remember that too, from somewhere.
fixes.why: The object-fronting is Russian syntax and sounds non-native here.

fixes.find: Behind us something sighs, and the coal comes down the face in a rustling wave.
fixes.replace: Behind us something sighs, and the coal comes along the face in a rustling wave.
fixes.why: The coal is moving along the longwall, not downward over the face.

fixes.find: Under the frame there's a hollow left, and he breathes in it.
fixes.replace: A hollow stays under the frame, and that's where he breathes.
fixes.why: “There's a hollow left” is a literal, awkward construction.

fixes.find: Seryoga surviving wasn't a clue to anything; I made that up myself.
fixes.replace: The fact that Seryoga survived didn't tell me anything; I made that up myself.
fixes.why: “Clue” adds a gamey detective register; the Russian is plainer and more self-accusing.

fixes.find: I run over the sleepers with the self-rescuer in my mouth.
fixes.replace: I run over the rail ties with the self-rescuer in my mouth.
fixes.why: The text uses American spelling; “rail ties” is clearer for the target reader than British “sleepers.”

fixes.find: I ran it in PE at college.
fixes.replace: I ran it in PE at technical school.
fixes.why: “Техникум” is not generic college; this also keeps the social setting sharper.

fixes.find: Down here every sleeper is higher than the last.
fixes.replace: Down here every tie is higher than the last.
fixes.why: Keeps the rail-term change consistent.

fixes.find: At four hundred meters I start counting sleepers so I won't count breaths.
fixes.replace: At four hundred meters I start counting ties so I won't count breaths.
fixes.why: Keeps the rail-term change consistent.

fixes.find: At five hundred I find I'm on my knees and don't remember getting down on them.
fixes.replace: At five hundred I'm on my knees and don't remember getting down on them.
fixes.why: Removes a filter-verb construction; the sentence is stronger directly.

fixes.find: My lamp shines on the roof, on a rusty lagging bar with "520" written on it in chalk.
fixes.replace: My lamp shines upward, on rusty roof lagging with "520" written on it in chalk.
fixes.why: “Lagging bar” is clunky; “roof lagging” is the natural mining phrasing.

fixes.find: Not a single sleeper yet.
fixes.replace: Not a single tie yet.
fixes.why: Keeps the rail-term change consistent.

fixes.find: The air in the crosscut stands still, like in a three-liter jar.
fixes.replace: The air in the crosscut stands still, trapped in a three-liter jar.
fixes.why: “Like in” is literal and weak; the image works better as an active compression.

fixes.find: Gas seeps in from the drift above, quiet as a cat into a kitchen.
fixes.replace: Gas seeps in from the drift above, quiet as a cat slipping into the kitchen.
fixes.why: The English simile needs the implied motion made explicit.

fixes.find: I don't notice until my arms go limp and the self-rescuer feels heavy and pointless, like a winter hat in May.
fixes.replace: I don't notice until my arms go limp and the self-rescuer feels heavy and useless, like a winter hat in May.
fixes.why: “Pointless” is abstract; the Russian means the thing feels needless/useless on the body.

fixes.find: I sat pressed against it with my back for that whole hour and never once turned around.
fixes.replace: I spent that whole hour with my back pressed to it and never once turned around.
fixes.why: Literal Russian syntax; the revised line is idiomatic and keeps the bodily memory.

fixes.find: The ventilation plan hanging in the assignment room I never studied properly; there was never time.
fixes.replace: I never really studied the ventilation plan hanging in the shift office; there was never time.
fixes.why: Russian topicalization plus “assignment room” read unnatural; “shift office” is clearer.

fixes.find: yelling that there's nothing in it to breathe.
fixes.replace: yelling that there's no air in it.
fixes.why: “Nothing in it to breathe” is literal and unidiomatic.

fixes.find: he fights me off like a drunk in a sobering-up cell and catches my mouthpiece with his elbow.
fixes.replace: he fights me off like a drunk in the drunk tank and elbows me in the mouthpiece.
fixes.why: “Sobering-up cell” is a calque; “catches my mouthpiece” also misdescribes the blow.

fixes.find: Only I've already breathed without it, twice, deep, like before a dive.
fixes.replace: But I've already breathed without it, twice, deep, like before a dive.
fixes.why: Sentence-initial “Only” in this sense is Russian connective logic, not natural English.

fixes.find: My head goes light.
fixes.replace: I get light-headed.
fixes.why: “Head goes light” is understandable but not idiomatic.

fixes.find: Down at the shaft bottom it smells of burning and warm iron.
fixes.replace: Down at the shaft bottom it smells of smoke and warm iron.
fixes.why: “Smells of burning” as a noun is awkward; “smoke” matches гарь here.

fixes.find: I take the one lying down under the arms.
fixes.replace: I take the man on the ground under the arms.
fixes.why: “The one lying down” is stiff in English action prose.

fixes.find: My face is burning from the inside, from the throat.
fixes.replace: My face burns from the inside, starting at the throat.
fixes.why: “From the throat” is a literal Russian attachment and reads incomplete.

fixes.find: Gray with dust, on blue tape, three turns, like a bandage. My three turns.
fixes.replace: Gray with dust, held on with blue electrical tape, three wraps, like a bandage. My three wraps.
fixes.why: “On blue tape” loses that it is taped over the sensor; “electrical tape” is the real object.

fixes.find: Seryoga is showing me Mishka on his phone, in the bobble hat.
fixes.replace: Seryoga is showing me Mishka on his phone, in a hat with a pom-pom.
fixes.why: “Bobble hat” is British; the glossary asks for neutral American spelling/wording.

fixes.find: whose three turns of tape those are.
fixes.replace: whose three wraps of tape those are.
fixes.why: Keeps the tape wording idiomatic and consistent with the earlier fix.

fixes.find: The back of my neck pulls me there, past this minute, to February, to that shift at this same junction.
fixes.replace: A pull at the back of my neck drags me there, past this minute, to February, to that shift at this same junction.
fixes.why: The original English makes the body part act like a subject; the revised line keeps the loop sensation.

fixes.find: I'm just laid down on the conveyor, and above, where the roof was, there's suddenly nothing.
fixes.replace: The blast simply lays me flat on the conveyor, and above, where the roof was, there's suddenly nothing.
fixes.why: “I'm just laid down” is unidiomatic passive phrasing.

fixes.find: The support sections fold one after another, like dominoes, with an iron clang, and my turn comes.
fixes.replace: The support sections fold one after another, like dominoes, with iron clangs, and my turn comes.
fixes.why: Several sections fold, so the sound should not be a single clang.

fixes.find: Plastic rustles in my fingers, a Maria-Ra bag that isn't here.
fixes.replace: Plastic rustles in my fingers, a Maria-Ra grocery bag that isn't here.
fixes.why: A light in-line cue tells an English reader Maria-Ra is a store bag without overexplaining.

fixes.find: Why I'm remembering it now I don't understand, but the back of my neck pulls me there like a sore tooth.
fixes.replace: I don't understand why I'm remembering it now, but the back of my neck aches like a sore tooth and pulls me there.
fixes.why: The fronted clause and the sore-tooth comparison are Russian-shaped in English.

fixes.find: The self-rescuer is breathing harder and harder, I'm hot, my mouth tastes sweetish, like caramel.
fixes.replace: Breathing through the self-rescuer gets harder and harder, I'm hot, my mouth tastes sweetish, like caramel.
fixes.why: In English the device “breathing” sounds accidental rather than bodily.

fixes.find: My arms don't stop obeying all at once; first my fingers, then my wrists.
fixes.replace: My arms don't give out all at once; first my fingers, then my hands.
fixes.why: “Кисти” are hands, not wrists; “stop obeying” is also a Russian calque.

fixes.find: holding a cable on hooks with one hand.
fixes.replace: holding on with one hand to a cable on hooks.
fixes.why: The original object order is clumsy; “holding on to” is the idiom.

fixes.find: The flashlight reaches half a meter and stops in the murk, and something white floats in the murk, in flakes.
fixes.replace: The flashlight reaches half a meter and stops in the murk; something white floats there, in flakes.
fixes.why: Removes the heavy repeated “murk” while keeping the limited visibility.

fixes.find: I swim on without the cable, by a memory of the plan that I don't have.
fixes.replace: I swim on without the cable, following a memory of the plan I don't have.
fixes.why: “By a memory” is not idiomatic English.

fixes.find: The rope at my waist snags on something and won't let me back.
fixes.replace: The rope at my waist snags on something and won't let me go back.
fixes.why: “Let me back” is elliptical in a way that sounds non-native here.

fixes.find: Everything like when I was seven. Black water, crowded, and right by my ear somebody starts counting.
fixes.replace: Everything is like when I was seven. Black water, no room, and right by my ear somebody starts counting.
fixes.why: “Crowded” implies people; тесно here is the cramped pressure of drowning.

fixes.find: whether to put in the pump.
fixes.replace: whether to set up the pump.
fixes.why: They are not installing a pump permanently; they are setting it up for use.

fixes.find: At twenty my helmet knocked against something under the ceiling, hollow, with emptiness inside it, and I swam on, down, after the cable.
fixes.replace: At twenty meters my helmet knocked against something under the ceiling, a hollow sound with empty space behind it, and I swam on, down, after the cable.
fixes.why: Restores “meters” and makes the air-pocket clue intelligible in English.

verdict: Партия в целом сильная: темп, телесность шахтёрских смертей и повторяющиеся детали в основном держатся. Самые частые проблемы — русская синтаксическая калька, чуть неточные технические/бытовые реалии и отдельные британизмы или неидиоматичные связки. Крупных смысловых провалов почти нет, но именно мелкие предлоги, порядок слов и термины местами выдают перевод.
